title: Some Questions Are Not Meant to Be Solved
author: Arthur C. Brooks
summary: Modern life tempts us to treat every human problem as technical, applying optimization mindsets to matters of meaning, love, faith, and beauty. These deepest questions cannot be solved like spreadsheets—they require contemplation, humility, mystery, and courage. Brooks reflects on how love can mature from passion into companionship in meaning-seeking, and how faith means accepting life's mystery not as an enemy but as part of the point. True leadership means understanding our lives more deeply, not just optimizing them.
points: Some of the most important things in life cannot be solved; they can only be lived.
One of the great confusions of modern life is treating every human problem as technical, when meaning requires a different part of ourselves.
Love can mature from initial passion into companionship in the search for meaning itself.
Faith does not mean having all the answers but accepting that mystery is part of the point.
Understanding our lives more deeply matters more than optimizing them.
quotes: Some of the most important things in life cannot be solved. They can only be lived. Love is like that. Beauty is like that. Faith is like that. And suffering is like that.
One of the great confusions of modern life is that we are tempted to treat every human problem as if it were technical. But meaning is not that kind of question.
At the beginning of love, there is passion. But if you are fortunate, and if you are faithful, that passion can become companionship in the search for meaning itself.
For me, faith does not mean having all the answers. It means accepting that much of life will remain a mystery—and that the mystery is not the enemy. It is part of the point.
We need to put technology in its proper place—and stop allowing it to crowd out the deepest experiences of being human.
This journey is not about optimizing our lives, but understanding them more deeply.” Archived from Arthur Brooks Newsletter on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
